title: Lamentations 2:11–19
context: The poet now speaks in the first person of tears: eyes fail, the heart is troubled, and grief is poured out because of the destruction of the daughter of the people, and because young children and infants swoon in the streets. They ask their mothers for grain and wine as they fail. The poet asks what can be said or compared to comfort the daughter of Jerusalem, whose breach is as big as the sea. False and foolish visions are charged to her prophets. Passers-by hiss; enemies boast that they have swallowed her up. The LORD has done what he planned, and has fulfilled his word commanded in the days of old. The wall of the daughter of Zion is told to let tears run down like a river, and to arise and cry out, pouring out the heart before the Lord, and lifting up hands for the life of the young children who faint for hunger at the head of every street. Famine and the children in the streets require utmost pastoral care: the verses should be reported briefly and soberly, without elaboration, without a lecture applied to other times. Wrath fulfilled and this grief are shared ground. The planned word of old may be compared, without harmonizing, with Deuteronomy 28, and the fall itself with 2 Kings 25 and Jeremiah 39 and 52. How God relates to the enemy who rejoices may, if needed, be compared with Judges 9:23.

verses.text: My eyes fail with tears. My heart is troubled. My bile is poured on the earth, because of the destruction of the daughter of my people, because the young children and the infants swoon in the streets of the city.
verses.arminianNotes:
“My eyes fail with tears. My heart is troubled.” The poet’s own body is now in the lament: tears, a troubled heart, and, in the verse’s own wording, bile poured on the earth, because of the destruction of the daughter of the people, and because the young children and the infants swoon in the streets of the city. The children’s collapse should be stated only as the verse states it, briefly and with care. The language of bile is the poet’s way of saying the grief is physically overwhelming; it needs no further description.

Arminian readers hear a first-person witness who cannot look without tears, and who names the children in the streets as the reason, a grief that should be received as grief.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers take the same failing eyes, troubled heart, and poured-out grief, because of the people’s destruction and because the young children and infants swoon in the streets.

Shared ground: the poet weeps, and the children are in the streets. The verse is left without added detail or a lecture.

verses.text: They ask their mothers, “Where is grain and wine?” when they swoon as the wounded in the streets of the city, when their soul is poured out into their mothers’ bosom.
verses.arminianNotes:
They ask their mothers, “Where is grain and wine?” when they swoon as the wounded in the streets, and when their soul is poured out into their mothers’ bosom. The question is a child’s question about food. It should be reported in that brief, sober form, without elaboration, and without any added scene. The mothers and the children are left where the verse leaves them.

Arminian readers hear the question as the poem’s sharpest famine-cry in this unit, a question that needs no commentary beyond its own words, and that the lament is right to record.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers take the same question, the swooning in the streets, and the soul poured out into the mothers’ bosom, as the poet’s account of the children’s hunger, to be left as brief as the line itself.

Shared ground: the children ask for grain and wine, and they fail. Pastoral restraint is the first duty of the notes.

verses.text: What shall I testify to you? What shall I liken to you, daughter of Jerusalem? What shall I compare to you, that I may comfort you, virgin daughter of Zion? For your breach is as big as the sea. Who can heal you?
verses.arminianNotes:
“What shall I testify to you? What shall I liken to you, daughter of Jerusalem?” The poet cannot find a comparison that would comfort the virgin daughter of Zion: “For your breach is as big as the sea. Who can heal you?” The breach as big as the sea is the measure of a wound past ordinary comfort. The title “virgin daughter of Zion” is a name for the people, and is left as such, without other comment.

Arminian readers hear a comforter at a loss, asking who can heal a breach that large, an honest limit on what words can do in this grief.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers take the same unanswered questions and the breach as big as the sea as the poet’s confession that comfort will not come by a comparison.

Shared ground: the wound is too large for ordinary likenesses. Who can heal her remains an open question in the verse.

verses.text: Your prophets have seen false and foolish visions for you. They have not uncovered your iniquity, to reverse your captivity, but have seen for you false revelations and causes of banishment.
verses.arminianNotes:
“Your prophets have seen false and foolish visions for you.” They have not uncovered iniquity, so as to reverse the captivity; they have seen false revelations and causes of banishment. The charge is that the visions did not expose the sin that needed exposing, and that they helped on the exile rather than turning it back. That is a shared, specific charge, not a new general contrast over prophecy.

Arminian readers hear a real failure of the prophets to uncover iniquity, a missed chance of reversal, which the poet now names as false and foolish vision.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers take the same false and foolish visions, the failure to uncover iniquity, and the revelations that were causes of banishment, as the poet’s verdict on the prophets who had spoken to her.

Shared ground: the visions were false, and they did not lead to a turning. The verse can stand without a new contrast of that kind.

verses.text: All that pass by clap their hands at you. They hiss and wag their head at the daughter of Jerusalem, saying, “Is this the city that men called ‘The perfection of beauty, the joy of the whole earth’?”
verses.arminianNotes:
All who pass by clap, hiss, and wag the head at the daughter of Jerusalem, saying, “Is this the city that men called ‘The perfection of beauty, the joy of the whole earth’?” The taunt quotes a former title in order to mock it. The poet records the passers-by, not a hymn of his own in those words.

Arminian readers hear the shame of a beauty now hissed at, a public scorn the city must bear, which belongs to the lament and does not need a reconstructed claim about the quoted title.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers take the same clapping, hissing, and wagging of heads, and the same mocking question about the city once called the perfection of beauty and the joy of the whole earth.

Shared ground: the city’s former praise has become a taunt. The traditions share the humiliation this verse records.

verses.text: All your enemies have opened their mouth wide against you. They hiss and gnash their teeth. They say, “We have swallowed her up. Certainly this is the day that we looked for. We have found it. We have seen it.”
verses.arminianNotes:
The enemies open the mouth, hiss, and gnash the teeth. They say, “We have swallowed her up. Certainly this is the day that we looked for. We have found it. We have seen it.” Their speech is triumph over a day long wanted. The poet lets them speak, and the boast is itself part of Zion’s grief.

Arminian readers hear the enemies’ satisfaction as a real wound added to the destruction, a day they looked for and now claim to have found, which the lament does not deny they have found.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers take the same opened mouths, the hissing and gnashing, and the boast “We have swallowed her up.” as the enemy’s own account of the day, recorded by the poet.

Shared ground: the enemies rejoice, and they say they have seen the day they wanted. Verse 17 will ascribe the fulfillment to the LORD.

verses.text: The LORD has done that which he planned. He has fulfilled his word that he commanded in the days of old. He has thrown down, and has not pitied. He has caused the enemy to rejoice over you. He has exalted the horn of your adversaries.
verses.arminianNotes:
“The LORD has done that which he planned.” The poet adds that the word commanded in the days of old has been fulfilled; she has been thrown down without pity; the enemy has been made to rejoice, and the horn of the adversaries has been exalted. The planning and the old word are shared ground: God has done what he said. Classical Arminians affirm that this prior word was truly known and purposed by God, not that the future was open or unknown to him. How the “days of old” relate to Deuteronomy 28, or to other warnings, should be named only by reference and left unharmonized. How God relates to the rejoicing enemy may be compared with the existing box at Judges 9:23, without restating it.

Arminian readers hear a fulfilled word and a planned throwing-down, which they can receive as the LORD’s faithful warning brought to pass, even while the verse remains a lament and not a treatise.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers take the same planned act, the fulfilled word from the days of old, the throwing-down without pity, and the enemy’s exalted horn, as the LORD’s own doing, which the poet now confesses.

Shared ground: the LORD has done what he planned. The traditions need not open a new contrast over that confession.

verses.text: Their heart cried to the Lord. O wall of the daughter of Zion, let tears run down like a river day and night. Give yourself no relief. Don’t let your eyes rest.
verses.arminianNotes:
“Their heart cried to the Lord.” Then the poet addresses the wall of the daughter of Zion: let tears run down like a river day and night. “Give yourself no relief. Don’t let your eyes rest.” The cry is to be unceasing. The “wall” is spoken to as if it could weep with the city; the image may be left as the poem’s address, without a forced explanation.

Arminian readers hear a summons to unending tears, a refusal of relief that matches the size of the breach, which the poet urges on Zion as the fitting work of this night of grief.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers take the same cried-out heart, and the charge to the wall of Zion to let tears run like a river day and night, without relief or rest for the eyes.

Shared ground: the unit turns from report to exhortation to weep. The traditions can share that call.

verses.text: Arise, cry out in the night, at the beginning of the watches! Pour out your heart like water before the face of the Lord. Lift up your hands toward him for the life of your young children, who faint for hunger at the head of every street.
verses.arminianNotes:
“Arise, cry out in the night, at the beginning of the watches!” She is told to pour out her heart like water before the face of the Lord, and to lift up her hands toward him “for the life of your young children, who faint for hunger at the head of every street.” The prayer is for the children’s life. The hunger at the street heads should be named only in the verse’s words, briefly and soberly, without elaboration.

Arminian readers hear a real call to night prayer, hands lifted to the Lord for the children’s life, the only help the poet can now urge, and a plea that is left as a plea.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers take the same rising in the night, the heart poured out like water before the Lord, and the hands lifted for the life of the young children who faint for hunger.

Shared ground: the poet sends Zion to prayer for the children. The hunger is named briefly, without being turned into a lecture.
